nodes.label: xmin as an EF Core concurrency token
nodes.rationale: xmin is a PostgreSQL system column holding the id of the transaction that last wrote the row; Postgres bumps it on every UPDATE for free, so it is a version counter with zero schema cost and no code to maintain. Marked IsConcurrencyToken() EF appends it to the UPDATE WHERE clause; zero rows matched raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Advantage over an application-maintained Version column: raw SQL outside EF still bumps it.

nodes.label: Bounded retry loop with re-read and re-decide
nodes.rationale: Three things are easy to get wrong: a fresh DbContext per attempt (reusing one keeps the stale entity tracked so the retry re-sends the same doomed UPDATE forever), re-reading AND re-deciding rather than just re-sending the write, and bounding the retries. Unbounded retry under heavy contention is a livelock — everything busy, nothing progressing. Jittered exponential backoff belongs in production.

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency pays in wasted work
nodes.rationale: Measured: 5 actors, 9 attempts, 4 conflicts, 0.0 ms waited. Nobody blocks anybody; the price of a collision is rework. It degrades under contention by doing N× the work for 1× the throughput rather than by corrupting data — a better failure mode, but still a failure mode, and one that only appears under load.

nodes.label: The hot row
nodes.rationale: One account everyone hits, a global counter, a shared inventory row. Every write conflicts with every other, so optimistic concurrency retry-storms. That is the signal to switch to pessimistic locking or to redesign the row so it stops being hot.
